extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of religious history, literary biography, and 17th-century English theology
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length literary and historical analysis of John Bunyan's spiritual life, Puritan theology, and the religious context of 17th-century England. The text offers descriptive and evaluative remarks about creeds, conversion, and religious character rather than procedural rules or formal checklists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge a creed by its effects on character
rubrics_metrics.description: We must judge of a creed by its effects on character, as we judge of the wholesomeness of food as it condues to bodily health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page argues that the truth or value of a religious doctrine should be assessed by the moral qualities and behaviours it produces in adherents (examples: horror of sin, enthusiasm for justice, purity, and manliness). This is presented as a central evaluative principle for religion and creeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puritan conception of salvation and its behavioural signs
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditions of acceptance were no longer sacraments or outward acts, but faith in what Christ had done; a complete self-abnegation, a resigned consciousness of utter unworthiness, and an unreserved acceptance of the mercy held out through the Atonement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puritan theology emphasizes inward faith and total self-abnegation. Although faith is primary, good works remain the necessary fruit and test of saving faith: 'Good works were the test of saving faith, and if there were no signs of them, the faith was barren.' The text uses this doctrine to explain observable standards for judging genuine religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of acceptance: sacramental/material vs faith/inward change
rubrics_metrics.description: Catholic (sacramental/material) view: sacraments and a changed corporeal element (e.g., Eucharist, baptism, penance) as means of grace; Protestant/Puritan view: rejection of material sacramental efficacy in favour of faith and inward change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page contrasts doctrinal standards for salvation: whether the atonement is efficacious materially (sacraments) or through faith. This contrast functions as a criterion for classifying religious approaches and for evaluating what constitutes legitimate religious assurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical religion/common ground: obligation to lead a moral life
rubrics_metrics.description: Where ambiguity exists between theological positions (e.g., Church of England compromise), the 'real truth of religion lies in what is common to the two theories, the obligation to lead a moral life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When doctrines are uncertain or compromise, the practical ethical obligation to moral conduct becomes the working standard for religion's value. The book treats this practical consequence as an evaluative yardstick for ecclesiastical compromise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of genuine conversion / earnestness
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable marks include: 'a great softness and tenderness of heart' and 'a great bending of my mind to a continual meditating on it' — persistent longing, prayerful attention, and inward fixation on eternity and the kingdom of heaven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists mental and affective dispositions (tenderness, sustained meditation, longing for conversion) as concrete indicators of authentic religious change. These are presented as tests to distinguish casual religion from deep conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-conquest and moral austerity as religious aims
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of it, so far as it affected action, was self-conquest: renunciation of pleasures, mortification, penance, and strictness in word and deed (examples: giving up dancing, music, ringing bells).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative treats renunciation of innocent amusements and rigorous self-discipline as characteristic fruits of earnest religion and as behavioural criteria by which contemporaries judged seriousness of faith. The account both endorses the moral beauty this produced and warns of excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity vs mere profession (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of words is repeated by multitudes who do not care to think what they are saying; mere profession without real conviction or transformation is hollow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns against outward lip-service and rote formulas, indicating that genuine religion must be substantiated by inward conviction and moral effects. Hypocrisy — repeating phrases without real feeling — is identified as a common defect and a negative evaluative criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger/limitation of exaggerated scruples
rubrics_metrics.description: Some scruples (e.g., extreme fears about harmless amusements or excessive self-accusation) may be 'exaggerated and fantastic' and potentially unhealthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While self-conquest is praised, the author notes that extreme scruples can be excessive and questions whether discarding them has been beneficial in the long term. This functions as a cautionary standard: spiritual strictness should be measured against psychological and social well-being.
